notes: The shortest Channel crossing and the most operator choice. DFDS takes vehicle passengers only, so foot passengers should look at P&O or Irish Ferries.
Lands closer to Belgium than Calais does, which suits Bruges, Ghent and the Belgian coast.
Restaurants and an onboard shop. A good gateway to Normandy from Sussex and the south coast.

dur: About 6 hours by day, about 6h45 overnight
notes: Sails to Ouistreham, the port for Caen. Both day and overnight sailings run.
Did not sail between October and the end of March last winter, so check dates before planning around it.

dur: Between 5 and 10 hours, depending on the sailing
notes: Runs on selected days, with up to two sailings on those days. The timetable is patchy, so look at the calendar first.

dur: About 8.5 hours by day, about 11.5 hours overnight
notes: The long way round the Channel Islands. Overnight sailings mean you can sleep on board.
The quickest way from Dorset to Normandy, and it now runs all year.

season: Seasonal, up to 6 days a week
notes: A high-speed sailing that calls at Guernsey on the way, about 3 hours in. It is the fastest Poole link to Brittany.

dur: About 6.5 hours by day, about 11 hours overnight
notes: Brittany from the far south west. Day and overnight sailings both run.
Only runs on limited dates, mainly outside the peak season. Check the calendar.
The quickest way to Spain by sea. It runs about twice a week, so build your dates around it.
Sources disagree on the exact time, between about 28 and 33 hours. Confirm on the timetable.

dur: About 30 to 36 hours, depending on direction
notes: An overnight crossing with cabins that lands in the Basque Country.

dur: About 7 hours, up to 8 or more overnight
notes: Day and overnight sailings with ensuite cabins. The shortest direct route to the Netherlands and a good start for Germany.
An overnight crossing with a cabin included in the ticket. Rotterdam has good road links to Belgium.
An overnight cruise ferry with daily sailings. Bring your car and take as much luggage as you like.

dur: About 3h15 to 3h30; the fast craft takes about 2 hours when it runs
notes: The busiest Irish Sea route, and the one with the most choice. From 28 September 2026 every passenger, including children, must show a valid passport to board.
The route for south Wales, the south west and the south of Ireland. Foot passengers can use selected Stena sailings. Passport required from 28 September 2026.
The southernmost Irish Sea crossing, serving Wexford, Waterford and Cork. Passport required from 28 September 2026.
Sails from Birkenhead on the Mersey. Northern Ireland is part of the UK, so this links two UK ports. Foot passengers can use selected sailings.

season: Up to 4 or 5 sailings a day
notes: The fast way to Belfast from Scotland. Stena uses the Old House Point terminal, north of the P&O one. Foot passengers can use selected sailings.
The shortest crossing to Northern Ireland. No cabins on board, and pets are allowed. P&O uses its own terminal south of the Stena one.

dur: About 2h45 by fast craft, up to 4h30 on the conventional ferry
season: A few sailings a week, year-round
notes: New from April 2026, replacing the Belfast link, which stopped in December 2025. It gives Northern Ireland a direct route to the island.
The fast craft only run from March to November, so winter sailings are on the conventional ferry.
The strongest year-round link to the island. Pets are not allowed on this route.

dur: About 10 hours overnight; some direct sailings take about 7.5
notes: Guernsey is served from Portsmouth by the former Condor routes, now run by Brittany Ferries. Overnight sailings back from Portsmouth give you a longer day in the UK.

season: Seasonal, up to 6 days a week
notes: The high-speed Voyager, the fastest ship in the Brittany Ferries fleet. It carries on to St Malo.
DFDS took over the Jersey routes in 2025. Cabins are available on the overnight sailings.
The quicker of the two UK links to Jersey, on a high-speed ferry.
The main car ferry to the Isle of Wight, leaving from Portsmouth International Port. Foot passengers usually take the FastCat to Ryde instead.
The FastCat catamaran for foot passengers and bikes, running from Portsmouth Harbour station to Ryde Pier Head.
A hovercraft rather than a ferry: the only year-round passenger hovercraft service in the world, and the fastest way across the Solent.
The quickest vehicle crossing to the island, through the mouth of the Lymington river and past Hurst Castle.

dur: About 30 minutes by Red Jet, about 1 hour by car ferry
notes: Two services: the Red Jet foot-passenger catamaran to West Cowes, and the vehicle ferry to East Cowes.

season: Mid-March to early November, Monday to Saturday
notes: The Scillonian III, the only passenger ship to the Isles of Scilly. It does not run in winter, when people fly or take the freight boat.
Sails on the MS Oldenburg, which also runs to Lundy from Bideford. Timetable depends on the tide.
The Arran ferry, one of the busiest on the CalMac network. Vehicle spaces sell out in summer, so book ahead.
The main link to the Isle of Bute, timed to meet trains at Wemyss Bay.
A car ferry across the Firth of Clyde to Dunoon on the Cowal peninsula.
The whisky island ferry to Islay. It shares its sailings with Port Ellen, so check which port a sailing calls at.
The southern Islay port, closest to the Laphroaig, Lagavulin and Ardbeg distilleries.
The Mull ferry, sailing from the mainland hub of Oban.
A small passenger ferry, with a vehicle ferry on the same route.
The long haul to Barra in the Outer Hebrides. It carries on to some other islands on certain days.
A scenic shortcut to Skye, popular on Highland road trips.
The link to South Uist in the Outer Hebrides. Times follow the tide.
A short hop from Skye to the Isle of Raasay.
Connects South Uist with Barra, so the two together make a link between the southern Outer Hebrides.
Links Mull with Ardnamurchan, the most westerly point of mainland Britain.
The Skye to Harris crossing, one leg of the triangle with Lochmaddy.
The Skye to North Uist crossing, one leg of the triangle with Tarbert.
Links Harris and North Uist across the Sound of Harris, a popular stretch for cyclists and island hoppers.
The main crossing to the Outer Hebrides, across the open Minch. Vehicle spaces sell out in July and August.

dur: About 12 hours direct, just over 14 hours via Orkney
notes: An overnight ferry and the longest internal ferry route in the UK, at about 216 miles. On some nights it calls at Kirkwall on the way.

season: Year-round, up to 6 sailings a day
notes: The route passes the Old Man of Hoy, the 137 metre sea stack, so it doubles as a scenic trip.
The quickest route to Orkney, crossing the Pentland Firth from near John o' Groats.
A passenger-only summer service that runs on a fast catamaran.
One of the internal Orkney ferries, running to the nearest of the North Isles.
The mainland link to Rousay, with onward sailings to Egilsay and Wyre.
The main ferry to Hoy and Flotta.
Links the Shetland mainland with the fishing island of Whalsay.
The Good Shepherd IV serves Fair Isle, Britain's most remote inhabited island. Sailings are limited and weather permitting.
The only inhabited island off the Northern Ireland coast, with a famous puffin colony in summer.
A short cross-border ferry between Northern Ireland and County Donegal. It saves a long drive around Lough Foyle. The Carlingford Lough ferry between Down and Louth is not running in 2026.
